subject: HEALTH
overview: Health 9 is a high-school health course built on skills: accessing valid information, analyzing influences, communicating, deciding, setting goals and advocating. Each day pairs a short reading or research task with a written product in the health journal; talk through every lesson, since discussion is where most learning happens. Preview sensitive weeks before teaching (eating disorders, suicide prevention, substance use, the CA Healthy Youth Act unit in weeks 19–25, violence and trafficking); you may opt out of sexual health instruction under Ed. Code 51938 and use the alternate project. Give unit tests closed-book and go over every missed item; projects are scored with 4-level rubrics in this guide.

weeks.prep: Health journal and colored pencils. Print 10 wellness scenario cards and a 20-item risk/protective list. Find or make a 30-question wellness self-inventory (5 questions each for physical, mental/emotional, social, environmental, intellectual, spiritual or use your own areas). Save the inventory — it is retaken in week 36.
misconceptions: Thinking health just means not being sick. Correct: WHO defines health as complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease.
Believing you can't influence your health. Correct: many risk factors (behaviors) are controllable.

days.guide: Read the WHO definition (1948): 'a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.' The child draws a triangle and lists three strengths and one weakness per side.

questions.q: What are the three sides of the health triangle?
questions.a: Physical, mental/emotional and social health.

days.guide: Draw a line from premature death to high-level wellness with neutral in the middle. The child places each card and writes a reason.

questions.q: Where does someone who exercises, sleeps well and has close friends fall?
questions.a: Toward high-level wellness, because healthy behaviors in several areas move them beyond simply not being sick.

days.guide: Sort the 20 items into risk vs. protective, then mark which are controllable.

questions.q: Classify: vaping, family history of diabetes, supportive friends, 9 hours of sleep.
questions.a: Vaping – controllable risk; family history of diabetes – uncontrollable risk; supportive friends – protective; 9 hours of sleep – controllable protective.

days.guide: The child completes the inventory and makes a bar graph of scores by area.

questions.q: Which area scored lowest and what might explain it?
questions.a: Answers vary; the child should cite specific inventory items.

days.guide: Child writes a one-page reflection; then give the vocabulary quiz.

questions.q: Define wellness.
questions.a: An active process of making choices toward a healthy and fulfilling life across all areas of health.

weeks.assessment_key: Vocabulary quiz key: 1) health – complete physical, mental, social well-being 2) wellness – active, ongoing state of choosing healthy behaviors 3) health triangle – physical, mental/emotional, social 4) wellness continuum – range from premature death to high-level wellness 5) risk factor – increases chance of harm 6) protective factor – decreases chance of harm 7) controllable risk – e.g., diet, activity, tobacco 8) uncontrollable risk – e.g., age, genetics 9) prevention – actions to stop problems before they start 10) health literacy – ability to find, understand and use health information. Reflection rubric (4): names strongest and weakest areas with evidence from the inventory and explains why each matters; 3 = both areas, thin explanation; 2 = one area; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Print a list of 15 values, a DECIDE worksheet and a 6-week goal tracker. Write 4 scenarios (staying up late before a test, skipping breakfast, party invite, sports injury).
misconceptions: Making decisions only on what feels good now. Correct: consider consequences for health, family, goals and values.
Writing goals that are too vague to track. Correct: SMART goals are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound.

days.guide: The child ranks values and explains how the top three affect health choices.

questions.q: How could valuing 'achievement' guide a health choice?
questions.a: Example: choosing to sleep 8–10 hours rather than staying up gaming because rest improves performance.

days.guide: Teach DECIDE: Define the problem, Explore options, Consider consequences, Identify values, Decide and act, Evaluate. Apply to the late-night scenario.

questions.q: What does the 'E' at the end of DECIDE mean?
questions.a: Evaluate — look back at the result and ask whether it was a good decision and what you learned.

days.guide: The child completes DECIDE worksheets for three scenarios with pros and cons.

questions.q: For a sports injury that still hurts, what's a healthy decision?
questions.a: Stop playing, tell the coach/parent and see a medical provider before returning.

days.guide: Rewrite five vague goals; then the child writes a SMART health goal and a 6-week tracker.

questions.q: Make 'get fit' SMART.
questions.a: Example: 'I will jog 20 minutes 4 days a week for 6 weeks and record each run on my tracker.'

days.guide: The child presents the goal; give the quiz.

questions.q: List the six DECIDE steps.
questions.a: Define, Explore, Consider, Identify values, Decide, Evaluate.

weeks.assessment_key: DECIDE worksheet: proficient if all six steps are completed with at least three options and realistic consequences. SMART goal: 1 pt per letter + tracker = 6. Quiz key: 1) Define the problem 2) Explore options 3) Consider consequences 4) Identify values 5) Decide and act 6) Evaluate 7) SMART = Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound 8) values guide decisions.

weeks.prep: Print a CRAAP checklist; pick four websites (.gov, .org, .com product). Find three viral health claims. Look up local clinic, pharmacy, urgent care and Covered California/Medi-Cal info. Write the Unit 1 test.
misconceptions: Trusting a source because it's popular or has many shares. Correct: check authority, evidence and purpose.
Using the ER for minor problems. Correct: ER is for emergencies; urgent care for non-life-threatening problems that need same-day care; primary care for routine and ongoing needs.

days.guide: The child scores each site with CRAAP and explains the most and least reliable.

questions.q: Why might a product site be less reliable?
questions.a: Its purpose is to sell, so information may be biased or exaggerated.

days.guide: The child traces three claims to their origins and judges each.

questions.q: What should you do with a health claim that has no traceable source?
questions.a: Treat it as unverified; don't share it, and check reputable sources such as CDC or NIH.

days.guide: Make a provider chart: primary care (checkups, ongoing care), specialists, urgent care, ER, school nurse, telehealth.

questions.q: Where should you go for a sprained ankle on a Saturday? For chest pain and trouble breathing?
questions.a: Sprained ankle – urgent care (or primary care next week if mild). Chest pain/trouble breathing – call 911/ER.

days.guide: Research and list local services with phone numbers.

questions.q: What is Covered California?
questions.a: California's health insurance marketplace where people buy plans, often with financial help; Medi-Cal is California's Medicaid program for low-income residents.

days.guide: Give the Unit 1 test.

questions.q: What does the 'A' for Authority ask?
questions.a: Who wrote or published it and are they qualified/credible?

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 test key: 1) WHO health definition 2) health triangle 3) wellness continuum 4) risk vs protective factors 5) DECIDE steps 6) SMART goal definition 7) rewrite vague goal correctly 8) CRAAP = Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose 9) .gov/.edu and medical organizations generally more reliable 10) when to use ER vs urgent care vs primary care 11) Medi-Cal = CA Medicaid; Covered California = marketplace. Directory: 4 = at least 6 services with addresses/phones including teen confidential services.

weeks.prep: Find a short nutrition video (e.g., USDA MyPlate). Open the MyPlate Plan tool. Gather measuring cups, cereal, rice, juice and nuts. Prepare a 3-day food log sheet and a 15-question quiz.
misconceptions: Thinking carbohydrates or fats are 'bad.' Correct: both are essential; choose whole grains and unsaturated fats.
Underestimating portions. Correct: measured servings are usually smaller than what people pour.

days.guide: Chart the six nutrients: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water with functions and sources.

questions.q: Which three nutrients provide energy and how many calories per gram?
questions.a: Carbohydrates (4 cal/g), protein (4 cal/g), fat (9 cal/g).

days.guide: Use MyPlate Plan with the child's info; record daily targets.

questions.q: Name the five MyPlate food groups.
questions.a: Fruits, vegetables, grains, protein foods, dairy.

days.guide: Measure recommended portions (1 cup cereal, ½ cup cooked rice = 1 oz-eq, ½ oz nuts = 1 oz-eq protein, 1 cup juice) and compare to usual servings.

questions.q: How much cooked rice counts as 1 ounce-equivalent of grains?
questions.a: ½ cup.

days.guide: Start the 3-day food log with food groups and portions.

questions.q: Why log drinks too?
questions.a: Beverages add calories and sugar (soda, juice) and count toward dairy/fruit groups.

days.guide: Compare log to targets; give the quiz.

questions.q: What are the main functions of protein?
questions.a: Building and repairing tissues, making enzymes and hormones, supporting immune function.

weeks.assessment_key: Nutrient quiz key (15): carbs – main energy; protein – growth/repair; fats – energy storage, vitamin absorption (A, D, E, K), cell membranes; vitamins – regulate body processes; minerals – e.g., calcium for bones, iron for blood; water – temperature regulation, transport; calories: carbs 4, protein 4, fat 9; fiber is a carbohydrate; MyPlate groups (5); half of grains whole; half plate fruits and vegetables. 12/15 proficient. Food-log comparison: compares each group to targets and names one change.

weeks.prep: Collect five packaged food labels (two cereals, two drinks, one snack), a sugar bowl, teaspoon, a can of soda and a sports drink. Read the Dietary Guidelines for Americans executive summary. Prepare a 10-question label practical with two unfamiliar labels and write your own answers from those labels.
misconceptions: Thinking %DV is the percentage of the food that is that nutrient. Correct: %DV shows how much one serving contributes to a day's recommended amount on a 2,000-calorie diet.
Ignoring serving size. Correct: all numbers are per serving; eating two servings doubles everything.

days.guide: Annotate a label: serving size and servings per container, calories, %DV, added sugars, sodium. Teach 5/20: 5% DV or less is low, 20% or more is high.

questions.q: A cereal has 25% DV sodium per serving. Is that high or low?
questions.a: High (20% or more).

days.guide: Compare pairs and choose the healthier option with label evidence (fiber, added sugar, sodium, saturated fat).

questions.q: Cereal A: 3 g fiber, 12 g added sugar; Cereal B: 6 g fiber, 4 g added sugar. Which is healthier?
questions.a: Cereal B — more fiber and less added sugar.

days.guide: Measure sugar: grams ÷ 4 = teaspoons. A 12-oz cola with about 39 g sugar ≈ 10 tsp; a 20-oz sports drink with about 34 g ≈ 8.5 tsp.

questions.q: A drink has 52 g sugar. How many teaspoons is that?
questions.a: 52 ÷ 4 = 13 teaspoons.

days.guide: Read the key recommendations and the child summarizes four in their own words.

questions.q: What do the Dietary Guidelines say about added sugars and sodium?
questions.a: Limit added sugars to less than 10% of calories per day starting at age 2, and sodium to less than 2,300 mg per day for ages 14+ (lower for younger children).

days.guide: Give the label practical.

questions.q: If a serving is 1 cup with 150 calories and you eat 2½ cups, how many calories?
questions.a: 375 calories.

weeks.assessment_key: Label practical: score against your answer sheet for the two labels; typical items: serving size, servings per container, calories per serving and for the whole package (calories × servings), %DV of sodium (high/low using 5/20), added sugar in teaspoons (g ÷ 4), fiber, which label is healthier and why. 8/10 = proficient.

weeks.prep: Parental preview: eating disorders and body image. Find a media-literacy lesson with edited vs. unedited images (e.g., Dove Self-Esteem Project) and the KidsHealth article 'Eating Disorders.' Avoid discussing specific weights or calorie numbers. Watch for warning signs in your own teen.
misconceptions: Believing eating disorders are about vanity or only affect thin girls. Correct: they are serious mental illnesses with among the highest death rates of any mental illness, affecting all genders and sizes.
Thinking crash diets work. Correct: severe restriction slows metabolism, causes muscle loss and usually leads to regain and possible disordered eating.

days.guide: Explain energy in vs. out and growth needs. The child estimates the energy cost of three activities using a chart (e.g., about 8–10 calories/min running vs. about 1–2 at rest, varying by body size).

questions.q: Why do teens need more energy than many adults?
questions.a: Rapid growth in height, muscle and bones plus activity increase energy needs.

days.guide: Compare images and write how filters/edits shape body expectations.

questions.q: How can filtered images affect body image?
questions.a: They set unrealistic standards, leading to comparison, dissatisfaction and sometimes unhealthy dieting.

days.guide: Read the article; chart anorexia, bulimia, binge eating disorder (and ARFID): signs and health effects.

questions.q: Name two health effects of anorexia.
questions.a: Slow heart rate, low blood pressure, bone loss (osteoporosis), loss of periods, fatigue, organ damage; it can be fatal.

days.guide: Evaluate three fad diets for teens; discuss why crash diets backfire.

questions.q: Why are detox teas not recommended?
questions.a: Many are laxatives or diuretics causing water loss and dehydration, not fat loss; the liver and kidneys already detox the body.

days.guide: Child writes the letter; give a short quiz.

questions.q: Name two places to get help for an eating disorder.
questions.a: A parent or trusted adult, doctor, school counselor, NEDA/ANAD helpline resources.

weeks.assessment_key: Letter rubric: 4 = names specific warning signs observed, expresses concern with I-statements, avoids blame/appearance comments, gives two valid help sources and encourages telling an adult; 3 = accurate but one element missing; 2 = vague; 1 = inaccurate. Quiz key: energy balance; edited images unrealistic; anorexia/bulimia/BED definitions; eating disorders are mental illnesses; crash diets slow metabolism.

weeks.prep: Gather cereal boxes or online food ads, a food thermometer, and a list of safe temperatures. Write a 6-question food safety quiz.
misconceptions: 'Health halo' — thinking 'natural,' 'organic' or 'multigrain' means healthy. Correct: check the label.
Thinking food is safe if it smells fine. Correct: many pathogens don't change smell; follow time and temperature rules.

days.guide: Analyze three ads or boxes for techniques and target audience.

questions.q: What is a 'health halo'?
questions.a: When one healthy-sounding claim ('gluten-free,' 'made with real fruit') makes people think the whole product is healthy.

days.guide: Research caffeine content and FDA regulation of supplements (not approved before sale); write a consumer warning.

questions.q: Why can't you assume a supplement is safe?
questions.a: Supplements don't need FDA approval before being sold; the FDA acts after problems are reported, and products may contain hidden ingredients.

days.guide: Teach Clean, Separate, Cook, Chill. Check temperatures while cooking: poultry 165°F, ground meats 160°F, whole cuts of beef/pork 145°F with 3-minute rest, leftovers 165°F.

questions.q: What's the safe internal temperature for ground beef?

days.guide: Audit fridge (40°F or below), freezer (0°F), cutting boards and leftovers (eat within 3–4 days).

questions.q: How long can leftovers stay in the fridge?
questions.a: 3–4 days.

days.guide: The child creates a counter-ad; give the quiz.

questions.q: What is the 'danger zone'?
questions.a: 40°F–140°F, where bacteria multiply quickly; don't leave food out more than 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F).

weeks.assessment_key: Food-safety quiz key: 1) Clean, Separate, Cook, Chill 2) poultry 165°F 3) ground meat 160°F 4) fridge ≤40°F 5) danger zone 40–140°F, 2-hour rule 6) leftovers 3–4 days. Counter-ad: 4 = uses two persuasive techniques accurately for a healthy food, clear audience and message.

weeks.prep: Gather an activity log and grocery flyer. Plan to cook together one day. Write the Unit 2 test.
misconceptions: Thinking teens need less sleep than kids. Correct: teens need 8–10 hours; their body clock shifts later.
Believing only sports count as activity. Correct: any moderate-to-vigorous movement (walking fast, biking, dancing) counts.

days.guide: Teach 60 minutes daily of moderate-to-vigorous activity with muscle- and bone-strengthening 3 days/week. Log today.

questions.q: What are the activity guidelines for teens?
questions.a: At least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity daily, mostly aerobic, with vigorous, muscle-strengthening and bone-strengthening activity at least 3 days a week each.

days.guide: Read about teen sleep (8–10 hours) and design a sleep-hygiene routine.

questions.q: Name three sleep-hygiene habits.
questions.a: Consistent bedtime/wake time, no screens 30–60 minutes before bed, cool dark room, limit caffeine after noon, avoid long late naps.

days.guide: Plan three days of balanced meals on a budget.

questions.q: How can you lower cost while staying balanced?
questions.a: Use beans, eggs, frozen produce, store brands and compare unit prices.

days.guide: Cook one meal; photograph and label food groups.

questions.q: Does your meal include at least three food groups?
questions.a: Answers vary; check the labeled photo.

days.guide: Give the Unit 2 test and collect the plan.

questions.q: What is the 5/20 rule?
questions.a: 5% DV or less is low; 20% DV or more is high.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 2 test key: six nutrients and functions; calories per gram (4/4/9); MyPlate groups; serving size and %DV; 5/20 rule; grams sugar ÷ 4 = tsp; added sugar <10% calories; sodium <2,300 mg; energy balance; eating disorder types; marketing techniques; supplements not FDA-approved; Clean/Separate/Cook/Chill; temps 165/160/145; 60 min activity; 8–10 hours sleep. Plan: proficient = three balanced days, budget, activity and sleep components.

weeks.prep: Health journal; find a list of mental wellness signs (e.g., NAMI or Mental Health America) and an emotion wheel. Choose a short biography of someone who overcame adversity (e.g., Malala Yousafzai, Simone Biles, Temple Grandin).
misconceptions: Thinking mental wellness means always being happy. Correct: it means coping with normal stresses, functioning and having a range of emotions.
Confusing self-esteem with arrogance. Correct: healthy self-esteem is realistic respect for yourself.

days.guide: Brainstorm signs, then compare to the organization's list.

questions.q: Name three signs of good mental health.
questions.a: Coping with stress, healthy relationships, expressing emotions appropriately, adapting to change, feeling purpose, asking for help when needed.

days.guide: Use the emotion wheel to name feelings and body cues.

questions.q: What body cues might come with anxiety?
questions.a: Racing heart, tight chest, sweaty hands, stomachache, shallow breathing, muscle tension.

days.guide: The child lists 10 strengths; a family member adds three.

questions.q: Why does naming strengths help?
questions.a: It builds realistic self-esteem and confidence, which supports resilience.

days.guide: Read the biography; identify protective factors.

questions.q: What protective factors helped the person?
questions.a: Answers vary by biography; e.g., Malala — supportive father, education, purpose and global support network.

days.guide: Child writes the reflection.

questions.q: Name two resilience skills.
questions.a: Problem solving, positive self-talk, seeking support, flexible thinking, self-care.

weeks.assessment_key: Resilience reflection rubric: 4 = specific setback, at least two resilience skills used or planned, connection to protective factors, insight about growth; 3 = setback and one skill; 2 = general description; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Timer, journal, and a fight-or-flight diagram. Find guided scripts for box breathing, progressive muscle relaxation and 5-4-3-2-1 grounding. Write a short quiz.
misconceptions: Thinking all stress is bad. Correct: eustress (positive stress) motivates; chronic distress harms health.
Trying to control everything. Correct: focus effort on controllable stressors; use coping for uncontrollable ones.

days.guide: Diagram: stressor → hypothalamus → adrenal glands release adrenaline (epinephrine) and cortisol → heart rate, breathing, blood pressure up, digestion slows, muscles tense.

questions.q: Which two hormones are released in the stress response?
questions.a: Adrenaline (epinephrine) and cortisol.

days.guide: List and rate stressors; sort controllable vs. not.

questions.q: Is 'a big test Friday' controllable?
questions.a: Partly — you can't change the test, but you can control studying, sleep and preparation.

days.guide: Practice each technique (box breathing 4-4-4-4) and rate them.

questions.q: Describe box breathing.
questions.a: Inhale 4 counts, hold 4, exhale 4, hold 4; repeat several times.

days.guide: Build a balanced weekly schedule.

questions.q: Why schedule downtime?
questions.a: Rest and fun reduce stress and prevent burnout.

days.guide: Make the toolkit card; give the quiz.

questions.q: What's the difference between eustress and distress?
questions.a: Eustress is positive, motivating stress (e.g., before a game); distress is negative stress that feels overwhelming and can harm health.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) stressor definition 2) adrenaline and cortisol 3) fight-or-flight body changes 4) eustress vs distress 5) chronic stress effects: sleep problems, weakened immunity, headaches 6) box breathing steps 7) 5-4-3-2-1 = 5 things you see, 4 touch, 3 hear, 2 smell, 1 taste. Toolkit: 5 healthy strategies with when to use each.

weeks.prep: Computer; NAMI/NIMH fact sheets on anxiety, depression, ADHD and PTSD. Prepare 12 myth/fact statements. Pick a TV show or movie clip that portrays mental illness.
misconceptions: Believing people with mental illness are violent. Correct: they are more likely to be victims of violence than perpetrators.
Thinking therapy is only for 'serious' problems. Correct: therapy helps with many everyday challenges.

days.guide: Complete the symptom/treatment chart.

questions.q: What is PTSD?
questions.a: Post-traumatic stress disorder: after a traumatic event, symptoms like flashbacks, nightmares, avoidance, being easily startled last more than a month; treated with trauma-focused therapy and sometimes medication.

days.guide: Sort myths/facts and correct each myth.

questions.q: Myth or fact: Mental illness is rare.
questions.a: Myth — about 1 in 5 U.S. adults and many teens experience a mental illness each year.

days.guide: Explain counseling, CBT (changing thought patterns and behaviors), medication, support groups.

questions.q: What does CBT focus on?
questions.a: Identifying and changing unhelpful thoughts and behaviors to improve feelings.

days.guide: Analyze the portrayal and how it could affect help-seeking.

questions.q: How can inaccurate portrayals affect people?
questions.a: They reinforce stereotypes and shame, making people less likely to seek help.

days.guide: The child designs the poster.

questions.q: Give one help resource for a poster.
questions.a: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (call/text 988), school counselor, NAMI HelpLine.

weeks.assessment_key: Poster rubric: 4 = at least two accurate facts, one myth corrected, person-first language, a help resource, clear anti-stigma message; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = one fact, no resource; 1 = inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Parental preview: suicide prevention. Read 988lifeline.org warning signs. Prepare role-play cards and a blank safety plan (Stanley-Brown style: warning signs, coping strategies, people/places, adults to ask, professionals, making environment safe). If your teen discloses suicidal thoughts, stay with them and call/text 988.
misconceptions: Thinking a friend's suicidal talk should be kept secret. Correct: always tell a trusted adult.
Believing a sudden calm after depression means they're better. Correct: sudden calm can be a warning sign if a person has decided on a plan.

days.guide: List warning signs (talking about wanting to die, hopelessness, withdrawing, giving away possessions, increased substance use) and risk factors (previous attempt, depression, access to lethal means, loss).

questions.q: Name three warning signs of suicide.
questions.a: Talking about wanting to die or being a burden, searching for means, withdrawing, extreme mood swings, giving away possessions, saying goodbye, increased substance use.

days.guide: Teach ACT: Acknowledge (take it seriously, ask directly), Care (listen, show concern), Tell (a trusted adult). Role-play.

questions.q: What does ACT stand for?
questions.a: Acknowledge, Care, Tell.

days.guide: Save 988 and Crisis Text Line (text HOME to 741741); list three trusted adults.

questions.q: What happens when you call or text 988?
questions.a: You reach a trained crisis counselor 24/7, free and confidential.

days.guide: The child completes a personal safety and support plan.

questions.q: Why include coping strategies and people in a plan?
questions.a: When distressed it's hard to think clearly; a written plan provides steps and contacts ready to use.

days.guide: Give scenario questions.

questions.q: A friend texts 'I won't be a problem anymore.' What do you do?
questions.a: Take it seriously: reply and ask directly if they're thinking about suicide, tell a trusted adult immediately and call 911 if they're in immediate danger; share 988.

weeks.assessment_key: Scenario key: each response should Acknowledge (ask directly), Care (listen, don't judge), Tell (adult now; 911 if immediate danger); never keep secret; never leave someone at immediate risk alone. Support plan: 4 = personal warning signs, 3 coping strategies, 2 people/places, 3 adults, 988/741741, safe-environment step.

weeks.prep: Phone for screen-time tracking; role-play scenarios for I-messages, active listening and a family conflict. Write the Unit 3 test. Look up California's Safe Place to Learn Act and Seth's Law (AB 9, 2011).
misconceptions: Thinking cyberbullying isn't real bullying. Correct: it is repeated harm through digital means and can be more pervasive.
Believing conflict resolution means one person wins. Correct: aim for win-win solutions.

days.guide: Define four forms of bullying; explain CA law (Seth's Law) requires schools to have anti-bullying policies and respond to reports.

questions.q: What is relational bullying?
questions.a: Harming someone's relationships or reputation — exclusion, rumors, manipulating friendships.

days.guide: Track screen time and rate mood after each app.

questions.q: Which app made you feel best or worst, and why?
questions.a: Answers vary; look for honest evaluation.

days.guide: Teach I-messages ('I feel __ when __ because __') and active listening (eye contact, paraphrase, ask questions). Role-play three times.

questions.q: Change 'You never listen!' into an I-message.
questions.a: 'I feel frustrated when I'm interrupted because I want to finish my thought.'

days.guide: Apply a six-step model: cool down, each tells their side, identify the problem, brainstorm solutions, choose win-win, follow up.

questions.q: Why cool down first?
questions.a: Strong emotions block clear thinking and escalate conflict.

days.guide: Give the Unit 3 test.

questions.q: What's active listening?
questions.a: Fully focusing on the speaker, showing interest, and paraphrasing to check understanding.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 3 test key: signs of mental wellness; emotion/body cues; resilience; adrenaline and cortisol; eustress vs distress; coping strategies; anxiety, depression, ADHD, PTSD symptoms; CBT; stigma; suicide warning signs; ACT; 988/741741; four bullying types; Seth's Law; I-message structure; conflict resolution steps.

weeks.prep: Brain diagram (reward pathway: ventral tegmental area → nucleus accumbens → prefrontal cortex) and NIDA 'Drugs, Brains, and Behavior' materials. Short quiz.
misconceptions: Thinking addiction only happens with illegal drugs. Correct: alcohol, nicotine and prescription drugs are addictive.
Believing the teen brain is fully mature. Correct: the prefrontal cortex develops into the mid-20s, so teens are more vulnerable to addiction.

days.guide: Label the reward pathway; explain drugs cause large dopamine surges that reinforce use.

questions.q: What role does dopamine play?
questions.a: It signals reward and teaches the brain to repeat a behavior; drugs flood the system with dopamine, strongly reinforcing use.

days.guide: Read NIDA on adolescent brains and summarize the prefrontal cortex's role.

questions.q: What does the prefrontal cortex do?
questions.a: Planning, judgment, impulse control and decision making.

days.guide: Flowchart: use → misuse → tolerance → dependence (withdrawal) → addiction.

questions.q: What is withdrawal?
questions.a: Uncomfortable physical/mental symptoms when a drug is stopped after dependence develops.

days.guide: Discuss genetics (about 40–60% of risk), environment and early use.

questions.q: Why does early use increase addiction risk?
questions.a: The developing brain adapts more readily, so earlier use is linked to higher rates of later addiction.

days.guide: Child writes the explanation; give the quiz.

questions.q: Is addiction curable or treatable?
questions.a: Treatable and manageable like other chronic diseases; relapse is possible.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: dopamine; reward pathway; prefrontal cortex – judgment/impulse control, matures mid-20s; tolerance; dependence/withdrawal; addiction = chronic relapsing brain disease; risk factors: genetics, environment, early use. Paragraph: 4 = accurate, simple, mentions brain changes and treatment.

weeks.prep: Computer; vape and tobacco ad examples; Kick It California (1-800-300-8086; kickitca.org). Short quiz.
misconceptions: Thinking vaping is harmless water vapor. Correct: aerosol contains nicotine, ultrafine particles, heavy metals (nickel, lead), flavoring chemicals like diacetyl and volatile organic compounds.
Believing you can't get addicted from occasional vaping. Correct: nicotine is highly addictive and teens can become dependent quickly.

days.guide: Research effects: addiction, harm to attention/learning, mood, increased heart rate; long-term lung and heart disease; EVALI lung injury (2019, linked mainly to THC vapes with vitamin E acetate).

questions.q: How does nicotine affect the teen brain?
questions.a: It harms parts that control attention, learning, mood and impulse control and primes the brain for other addictions.

days.guide: Analyze an aerosol ingredient list.

questions.q: Name two harmful substances in vape aerosol.
questions.a: Nicotine, heavy metals (nickel, tin, lead), ultrafine particles, volatile organic compounds, diacetyl, formaldehyde.

days.guide: Analyze ads for youth techniques.

questions.q: Name two techniques that target teens.
questions.a: Candy/fruit flavors, sleek tech-like designs, influencers, social media, colorful packaging.

days.guide: Tobacco 21 (since 2016, must be 21 to buy tobacco/vapes in CA); flavored tobacco ban (Prop 31, 2022). Find quit resources.

questions.q: What is the minimum age to buy tobacco in California?

days.guide: Child creates a counter-marketing post; quiz.

questions.q: Name a free quit resource for California teens.
questions.a: Kick It California (1-800-300-8086 or text 'Quit Vaping' to 66819), or This is Quitting by Truth Initiative.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: nicotine addictive, harms teen brain; aerosol contains heavy metals/chemicals; EVALI; marketing tactics; Tobacco 21; flavored ban (Prop 31); Kick It California. Post: 4 = accurate fact, exposes a tactic, clear audience, call to action.

weeks.prep: Computer; BAC factor chart; DMV handbook excerpt. Party scenario. Quiz.
misconceptions: Believing you can 'sleep it off' safely after heavy drinking. Correct: BAC can keep rising; a person with alcohol poisoning may stop breathing or choke on vomit.
Thinking cold showers or coffee sober you up. Correct: only time lowers BAC.

days.guide: Trace: mouth → stomach (~20% absorbed) → small intestine (~80%) → bloodstream → brain, liver (metabolizes), heart.

questions.q: Which organ metabolizes most alcohol?
questions.a: The liver.

days.guide: Factors: amount, time, body size, sex, food, carbonation; liver processes about one standard drink per hour.

questions.q: What is a standard drink?
questions.a: About 14 g of pure alcohol: 12 oz beer (5%), 5 oz wine (12%), 1.5 oz spirits (40%).

days.guide: Signs of alcohol poisoning: confusion, vomiting, seizures, slow/irregular breathing, blue-tinged or pale skin, low body temp, can't wake. Steps: call 911, don't leave alone, turn on side, don't give coffee or a cold shower.

questions.q: Name the acronym for alcohol poisoning signs.
questions.a: One common one is PUBS (or CUPS): Puking while passed out, Unresponsive, Breathing slow/irregular, Skin cold/blue/clammy. Any sign = call 911.

days.guide: Under-21 driver limit 0.01%; adults 0.08%; minor in possession penalties; license suspension; social host liability.

questions.q: What happens to a CA driver under 21 with BAC of 0.01% or more?
questions.a: One-year license suspension (zero-tolerance law), and higher BACs bring DUI charges.

days.guide: Use DECIDE on the party scenario; give the quiz.

questions.q: A friend passed out at a party and is breathing irregularly. What do you do?
questions.a: Call 911, stay with them, roll them onto their side, don't let them 'sleep it off.'

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: liver metabolizes alcohol; only time lowers BAC; standard drink = 14 g alcohol; BAC factors; alcohol poisoning signs and 911; CA under-21 limit 0.01% with 1-year suspension; adult 0.08%. Scenario: uses all DECIDE steps and chooses a safe, legal option.

weeks.prep: Parental preview: overdose. CDPH/DEA 'One Pill Can Kill' materials; a naloxone training video; a step checklist. Find a medicine take-back location (pharmacy kiosk or DEA Take Back Day).
misconceptions: Thinking pills bought online or from friends are real. Correct: DEA reports a large share of counterfeit pills contain potentially deadly fentanyl.
Believing cannabis is harmless because it's legal for adults. Correct: it's illegal under 21 and high-potency THC harms memory, motivation and mental health.

days.guide: Research cannabis effects on memory, attention, motivation; high-potency products increase risk of addiction and psychosis; cannabis hyperemesis syndrome.

questions.q: Why is high-potency cannabis risky for teens?
questions.a: Higher THC increases risk of cannabis use disorder, anxiety, psychosis and impaired memory and learning.

days.guide: Explain misuse (taking someone else's, wrong dose, to get high) and safe disposal (take-back kiosks; FDA guidance otherwise).

questions.q: How should leftover prescription painkillers be disposed of?
questions.a: At a drug take-back site or pharmacy kiosk; if none, follow FDA instructions (some on the flush list, others mixed with coffee grounds/cat litter in a sealed bag in trash).

days.guide: Explain fentanyl is 50x stronger than heroin; 2 mg can be lethal; counterfeit pills look like real ones.

questions.q: Why 'one pill can kill'?
questions.a: A single counterfeit pill can contain a lethal dose of fentanyl.

days.guide: Practice: check responsiveness, call 911, give naloxone in one nostril, rescue breathing, recovery position, second dose after 2–3 minutes, stay.

questions.q: Can naloxone hurt someone who isn't overdosing on opioids?
questions.a: No — it has no effect without opioids present; it's safe to give if you suspect overdose.

days.guide: Give the scenario quiz.

questions.q: What are three signs of opioid overdose?
questions.a: Pinpoint pupils, unresponsive, slow or stopped breathing, blue/gray lips.

weeks.assessment_key: Overdose scenario quiz key: recognize signs (pinpoint pupils, unresponsive, slow/no breathing, blue lips); steps in order: shout/sternum rub → call 911 → naloxone → support breathing → recovery position → second dose after 2–3 min → stay; CA Good Samaritan law protects callers. Proficient: all signs and steps correct.

weeks.prep: Semester review packet with practice questions on units 1–4; role-play cards; semester exam; refusal-skills checklist (clear 'no,' reason, alternative, firm body language, leave if needed).
misconceptions: Thinking you need a complicated excuse to refuse. Correct: 'No thanks' is enough; repeat it and leave if needed.
Believing 'everyone is doing it.' Correct: most teens don't use substances (look up current Monitoring the Future data).

days.guide: Map influences and protective factors.

questions.q: Name one protective factor against teen substance use.
questions.a: Parental monitoring and communication, involvement in activities, clear family rules, strong school connection, friends who don't use.

days.guide: Role-play five refusal strategies.

questions.q: Demonstrate 'suggest an alternative.'
questions.a: 'Nah, let's go shoot hoops instead.'

days.guide: Create a PSA promoting a substance-free lifestyle.

questions.q: What makes a PSA persuasive?
questions.a: One clear message, accurate fact, target audience and call to action.

days.guide: Review units 1–4.

questions.q: What's the 5/20 rule?
questions.a: 5% DV or less is low; 20% DV or more is high.

days.guide: Give the semester exam and refusal role-play check.

questions.q: Name the DECIDE steps.
questions.a: Define, Explore, Consider, Identify values, Decide, Evaluate.

weeks.assessment_key: Semester exam key draws on Unit tests 1–3 keys plus: dopamine/reward; tolerance/dependence; nicotine effects; Tobacco 21; alcohol poisoning signs; BAC zero tolerance; fentanyl; naloxone steps. Refusal checklist (1 pt each): clear no, reason, alternative, firm voice/body language, exits if needed — 4–5 = proficient.

weeks.prep: Parental preview: this unit (weeks 19–25) is taught under the CA Healthy Youth Act. Read the notice and decide on opt-out (Ed. Code 51938); opted-out students do an alternate project (e.g., research on healthy friendships, communication and community health resources). Print a relationship continuum (loveisrespect.org) and behavior cards; choose a short fictional relationship to analyze.
misconceptions: Thinking jealousy and control show love. Correct: they are red flags for unhealthy or abusive relationships.

Believing consent is the absence of 'no.' Correct: California's affirmative consent standard (used for colleges, SB 967) means an affirmative, conscious, voluntary agreement that is ongoing and can be revoked; silence or lack of resistance is not consent.

days.guide: Review the notice together and discuss family values and expectations; record any opt-out.

questions.q: Who can you go to with questions during this unit?
questions.a: Parent/guardian, doctor, school nurse or counselor, other trusted adults.

days.guide: Sort behaviors onto the healthy–unhealthy–abusive continuum and list red flags.

questions.q: Place 'tells you who you can hang out with.'
questions.a: Unhealthy to abusive — controlling and isolating behavior is a red flag.

days.guide: Define affirmative consent; analyze scenarios.

questions.q: A person agreed to a kiss earlier but now pulls away. Is there consent?
questions.a: No — consent is ongoing and can be withdrawn at any time; stop.

questions.q: Can someone who is drunk or asleep consent?
questions.a: No — they are not able to give conscious, voluntary agreement.

days.guide: Write physical, emotional and digital boundaries and practice stating them.

questions.q: Give an example of a digital boundary and how to say it.
questions.a: 'I don't share my passwords. Please don't ask me to.'

days.guide: The child analyzes the fictional relationship; give a quiz.

questions.q: Name three characteristics of a healthy relationship.
questions.a: Respect, trust, honesty, equality, good communication, support for each other's independence.

weeks.assessment_key: Relationship analysis: 4 = identifies at least three healthy and three unhealthy behaviors with evidence, places them on the continuum, explains consent issues and recommends a resource; 3 = mostly complete; 2 = list without evidence; 1 = incomplete. Quiz key: continuum (healthy/unhealthy/abusive); red flags (jealousy, control, isolation, threats); affirmative consent = clear, voluntary, ongoing, revocable; incapacitated people cannot consent; boundaries are personal limits you can state.

weeks.prep: Labeled diagrams of the endocrine system and male and female reproductive anatomy (KidsHealth or a biology text). Prepare a labeling quiz.
misconceptions: Thinking the menstrual cycle is always exactly 28 days. Correct: 21–35 days is normal for adults (21–45 in teens), and cycles can be irregular in the first years.
Believing reproductive health exams are only for adults. Correct: teens should see a doctor for problems such as severe pain, missed periods or testicular pain/lumps.

days.guide: Explain hypothalamus → pituitary (LH, FSH) → ovaries (estrogen, progesterone) or testes (testosterone). Label glands: pituitary, thyroid, adrenals, pancreas, ovaries/testes.

questions.q: Which gland is called the 'master gland'?
questions.a: The pituitary gland.

days.guide: Label ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, vagina; describe the cycle: menstruation, follicular phase, ovulation (about day 14 of a 28-day cycle), luteal phase.

questions.q: What happens during ovulation?
questions.a: An ovary releases a mature egg into the fallopian tube.

days.guide: Label testes, scrotum, epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, prostate, urethra, penis and describe functions.

questions.q: Where is sperm stored and matured?
questions.a: In the epididymis.

days.guide: Discuss hygiene, HPV vaccine, testicular self-exam, menstrual products and when to see a doctor (severe cramps, no period by 15, lumps, pain).

questions.q: Why is the scrotum outside the body?
questions.a: Sperm production needs a temperature slightly cooler than body temperature.

days.guide: Give the labeling quiz and written cycle response.

questions.q: Why does menstruation occur?
questions.a: If the egg is not fertilized, estrogen and progesterone drop and the uterine lining sheds.

weeks.assessment_key: Anatomy quiz: 1 pt per correct label (female: ovary, fallopian tube, uterus, cervix, vagina; male: testis, scrotum, epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicle, prostate, urethra, penis). Written cycle response (4): menstruation (lining sheds), follicular phase (FSH, follicle matures, estrogen rises, lining thickens), ovulation (LH surge releases egg), luteal phase (progesterone maintains lining; if no fertilization, hormones drop → menstruation).

weeks.prep: Find media samples (ads, music, a movie scene). Read your school or co-op's anti-discrimination policy; note California Education Code 220 prohibits discrimination based on sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression and sexual orientation in schools.
misconceptions: Confusing sex, gender identity, gender expression and orientation. Correct: they are distinct concepts.
Thinking 'just joking' about identity is harmless. Correct: it contributes to harassment and poorer mental health.

days.guide: Define terms with a medically accurate glossary.

questions.q: Distinguish sex assigned at birth from gender identity.
questions.a: Sex assigned at birth is based on physical anatomy/biology; gender identity is a person's internal sense of their gender.

days.guide: Analyze gender stereotypes in ads and how they affect relationships.

questions.q: How might 'boys don't show feelings' affect relationships?
questions.a: It discourages communication and help-seeking, harming emotional intimacy and mental health.

days.guide: Discuss respect and school protections (Ed. Code 220, Seth's Law).

questions.q: Name one California protection for students.
questions.a: Schools must not discriminate based on gender identity, expression or sexual orientation and must address bullying and harassment.

days.guide: Compare media portrayals of relationships to healthy traits.

questions.q: What do romantic movies often show that's unhealthy?
questions.a: Grand gestures after ignoring 'no,' jealousy as love, possessiveness, no communication about consent.

days.guide: The child writes a reflection.

questions.q: How can media shape relationship expectations?
questions.a: Repeated portrayals normalize behaviors (jealousy, pressure) and create unrealistic standards.

weeks.assessment_key: Media analysis reflection: 4 = analyzes at least two specific media examples, identifies stereotypes or unhealthy messages, compares to healthy traits, uses terms accurately and respectfully; 3 = one example analyzed well; 2 = general opinion; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Fertilization and fetal development diagrams; sources on prenatal care (March of Dimes, ACOG). Read California's Safely Surrendered Baby Law (infant up to 72 hours old, at a hospital or designated safe-surrender site). Prepare a budget worksheet and quiz. Discuss the topic of pregnancy options with your values in mind; the curriculum presents legal options factually.
misconceptions: Thinking prenatal care can wait until late pregnancy. Correct: major organs form in the first trimester, often before a person knows they are pregnant.
Underestimating the cost of a baby. Correct: first-year costs typically run many thousands of dollars.

days.guide: Describe fertilization in the fallopian tube and implantation in the uterine lining about 6–10 days later.

questions.q: What is a zygote?
questions.a: The single cell formed when a sperm fertilizes an egg.

days.guide: Make the timeline: embryo weeks 3–8 (heart, brain, spinal cord form; heartbeat around week 5–6), fetus from week 9; 2nd trimester movement, hearing; 3rd trimester weight gain and lung maturation.

questions.q: When do most major organs form?
questions.a: During the embryonic period, about weeks 3–8 of development (first trimester).

days.guide: Research prenatal care and effects of alcohol (FASD), tobacco (low birth weight), drugs.

questions.q: What is FASD?
questions.a: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorders — lifelong physical, behavioral and learning problems caused by alcohol exposure before birth.

days.guide: Present parenting, adoption and abortion as legal options in California; explain the Safely Surrendered Baby Law.

questions.q: What does California's Safely Surrendered Baby Law allow?
questions.a: A parent or person with lawful custody can confidentially surrender a baby up to 72 hours old at a hospital or designated safe-surrender site without fear of arrest for abandonment.

days.guide: Complete the budget and quiz.

questions.q: List four first-year baby costs.
questions.a: Diapers, formula/food, clothing, car seat, crib, medical care, childcare, housing.

weeks.assessment_key: Budget activity: proficient if at least 8 categories are estimated with realistic monthly costs and a first-year total. Quiz key: fertilization in fallopian tube; implantation in uterus; organs form weeks 3–8; trimesters (~13/27/40 weeks); prenatal care and folic acid; FASD; Safely Surrendered Baby Law (72 hours).

weeks.prep: CDC 'Contraceptive Effectiveness' chart (typical-use failure rates). No demonstrations needed. Write a matching quiz.
misconceptions: Thinking withdrawal or 'the first time' can't cause pregnancy. Correct: pregnancy can occur any time sperm meet an egg; withdrawal has about a 20% typical-use failure rate.
Believing hormonal methods protect against STIs. Correct: only condoms reduce STI risk; abstinence eliminates it.

days.guide: Discuss abstinence as the only 100% effective method and reasons people choose it.

questions.q: Why is abstinence the only 100% method?
questions.a: No sexual contact means no exposure to sperm or sexually transmitted infections.

days.guide: Review all FDA-approved methods on the CDC chart.

questions.q: What are LARC methods?
questions.a: Long-acting reversible contraception: IUDs (hormonal and copper) and the implant, all over 99% effective.

days.guide: Compare methods by effectiveness, STI protection and access (in CA, minors can obtain contraception confidentially).

questions.q: Which methods protect against both pregnancy and STIs?
questions.a: Abstinence (100%); external and internal condoms reduce both risks. Using a condom plus another method ('dual protection') gives better pregnancy prevention and STI protection.

days.guide: Apply DECIDE to a sexual-health scenario.

questions.q: What values and consequences should be considered?
questions.a: Personal/family values, readiness, risk of pregnancy and STIs, emotional impact, goals, and partner's respect for consent.

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: Typical-use effectiveness of the pill?
questions.a: About 93% (about 7 pregnancies per 100 users per year).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key (approximate CDC typical-use effectiveness): abstinence 100%; implant >99%; IUD >99%; shot (Depo-Provera) 96%; pill/patch/ring 93%; external condom 87%; internal condom 79%; withdrawal 80%; fertility awareness 77–98%; spermicide 79%. STI protection: only condoms (and abstinence). Written answer: abstinence prevents both completely; condoms reduce risk of both.

weeks.prep: CDC STI fact sheets and HIV.gov basics; CDC GetTested locator (gettested.cdc.gov). Blank six-infection chart; 15-question quiz. Opt-out alternative: communicable disease project.
misconceptions: Thinking you'd know if you had an STI. Correct: many are asymptomatic; testing is the only way to know.
Believing an STI once cured can't come back. Correct: you can be reinfected.

days.guide: Research chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis (bacterial, curable with antibiotics), HPV and herpes (viral, treatable not curable).

questions.q: Which common STIs are curable?
questions.a: Chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis (and trichomoniasis), with the right antibiotics/medication.

days.guide: Explain HIV attacks CD4 (T helper) cells; untreated it can progress to AIDS. Transmitted by blood, semen, vaginal fluids, breast milk; not by saliva, hugging, sharing dishes or mosquitoes.

questions.q: How does HIV damage the immune system?
questions.a: It infects and destroys CD4 T cells, weakening the body's ability to fight infections.

days.guide: Prevention: abstinence, condoms, HPV vaccine, PrEP (daily pill or injection before exposure), PEP (within 72 hours after possible exposure), testing.

questions.q: What is the difference between PrEP and PEP?
questions.a: PrEP is taken before possible exposure to prevent HIV; PEP is an emergency medicine started within 72 hours after possible exposure.

days.guide: Use the CDC locator; note CA minors 12+ can consent to STI testing and treatment confidentially.

questions.q: Can a 15-year-old in California get an STI test without parental consent?
questions.a: Yes — minors 12 and older can consent to STI testing and treatment.

days.guide: Complete the chart; give the 15-question quiz.

questions.q: What does U=U mean?
questions.a: Undetectable = Untransmittable: a person with HIV who maintains an undetectable viral load on treatment does not transmit HIV sexually.

weeks.assessment_key: STI chart key: chlamydia – bacteria, often no symptoms, curable (antibiotics), condoms/abstinence, urine/swab test; gonorrhea – bacteria, often none or discharge/burning, curable (drug resistance rising), same prevention, urine/swab; syphilis – bacteria, painless sore then rash, curable (penicillin), blood test; HPV – virus, often none or warts, not curable but vaccine prevents, Pap/HPV test for cervical changes; herpes (HSV) – virus, painful blisters, treatable not curable (antivirals), swab/blood; HIV – virus, flu-like early then none, treatable with ART not curable, PrEP/condoms, blood/oral test. Quiz: 12/15 proficient.

weeks.prep: Parental preview: sexual violence and trafficking. Read Title IX basics, RAINN (1-800-656-4673) and Polaris/National Human Trafficking Hotline (1-888-373-7888, text 233733). List California minor-consent services. Write Unit 5 test; opted-out students submit the alternate project.
misconceptions: Thinking assault is usually by strangers. Correct: most sexual assaults are committed by someone the victim knows.
Believing victims are to blame for what they wore or drank. Correct: the perpetrator is always responsible.

days.guide: Define harassment and assault; explain Title IX protects students from sex-based discrimination including harassment, and schools must respond.

questions.q: What is Title IX?
questions.a: A 1972 federal law prohibiting sex-based discrimination, including sexual harassment and violence, in schools that receive federal funding.

days.guide: Recruitment tactics: false job/modeling offers, 'boyfriend' grooming, gifts, isolation, online contact; warning signs.

questions.q: Name two warning signs someone is being trafficked.
questions.a: An older 'boyfriend' controlling them, unexplained gifts/money, not controlling own ID or phone, signs of abuse, sudden absences, scripted answers.

days.guide: List hotlines and trusted adults.

questions.q: What is the RAINN hotline?
questions.a: National Sexual Assault Hotline: 1-800-656-HOPE (4673), or online.rainn.org.

days.guide: Explain California minor consent: 12+ for STI testing/treatment, outpatient mental health counseling (if mature enough), sexual assault care, drug/alcohol counseling; any age for pregnancy-related care and contraception.

questions.q: Can a minor get contraception confidentially in CA?
questions.a: Yes, at any age.

days.guide: Give the Unit 5 test.

questions.q: Who is responsible for a sexual assault?
questions.a: Only the perpetrator — never the victim.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 5 test key: healthy vs abusive relationships; affirmative consent; endocrine/puberty hormones; reproductive anatomy and menstrual cycle; definitions of sex, gender identity, expression, orientation; fertilization/implantation; prenatal care; Safely Surrendered Baby Law; abstinence 100%; method effectiveness; only condoms reduce STI risk; curable vs treatable STIs; PrEP/PEP; Title IX; RAINN and trafficking hotline; CA minor consent rules. Alternate project rubric: 4 = accurate, researched, cites sources, addresses healthy relationships and resources.

weeks.prep: Look up CDC WISQARS or 'Leading Causes of Death' for ages 15–19. Print a home safety checklist (falls, fire, poisoning, firearm storage). Find a 'drowning doesn't look like drowning' video. Read CA concussion law (AB 2127).
misconceptions: Thinking drowning involves splashing and yelling. Correct: drowning is usually quiet — head low, mouth at water level, no waving.
Believing you should 'play through' a ding to the head. Correct: any suspected concussion means removal from play that day.

days.guide: Analyze data: leading causes of death for teens are unintentional injuries (motor-vehicle crashes, poisoning/overdose), homicide and suicide.

questions.q: What is the leading cause of death for U.S. teens?
questions.a: Unintentional injuries (accidents), led by motor-vehicle crashes and, increasingly, drug overdoses.

days.guide: Complete the audit with the child: smoke alarms, fall hazards, medicines locked, chemicals labeled, firearms locked and unloaded with ammunition separate.

questions.q: How should firearms be stored?
questions.a: Unloaded, locked (safe or lock box/cable lock), with ammunition stored and locked separately.

days.guide: Watch the video, list signs and write rules.

questions.q: List two signs of drowning.
questions.a: Head low in the water with mouth at surface, head tilted back, glassy eyes, vertical body, not able to wave or call for help.

days.guide: Concussion signs: headache, dizziness, confusion, nausea, light sensitivity, memory problems. AB 2127: removed for the rest of the day, written clearance from a licensed health care provider, and a graduated return-to-play protocol of at least 7 days.

questions.q: What does California law require after a suspected concussion in high school sports?
questions.a: Removal from activity for the remainder of the day, evaluation and written clearance by a licensed health care provider, and a graduated return-to-play protocol of no less than 7 days.

days.guide: Present the audit and complete one fix.

questions.q: Why test smoke alarms monthly?
questions.a: Working alarms halve the risk of dying in a home fire; batteries die.

weeks.assessment_key: Home safety audit: 4 = checks falls, fire, poisoning, firearms, water; identifies three prioritized fixes with reasons and completes one; 3 = two areas missing detail; 2 = partial; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Role-play scenarios for de-escalation; loveisrespect.org cycle-of-abuse page; dating violence safety-plan template. Know how to report threats (Say Something app, school, 911).
misconceptions: Thinking abuse is only physical. Correct: it includes emotional, verbal, digital, sexual and financial abuse.
Believing the abuser will change after apologizing. Correct: apologies and 'honeymoon' periods are part of the cycle.

days.guide: Identify risk (exposure to violence, substance use, access to weapons) and protective factors (connected adults, conflict skills).

questions.q: Name one protective factor against violence.
questions.a: Strong family connection, positive adult mentors, involvement in activities, conflict-resolution skills.

days.guide: Role-play de-escalation and rate techniques.

questions.q: Name two de-escalation techniques.
questions.a: Calm, low voice; give space; listen and acknowledge; avoid blaming; walk away and get help.

days.guide: Teach the cycle: tension building → incident → reconciliation/honeymoon → calm, and warning signs.

questions.q: Describe the cycle of abuse.
questions.a: Tension builds, an abusive incident occurs, the abuser apologizes or promises change (honeymoon), a calm period follows, and the cycle repeats.

days.guide: Discuss weapons and gang dangers and how to report threats.

questions.q: If you hear someone plans to bring a weapon to school, what do you do?
questions.a: Tell a trusted adult immediately or use an anonymous tip line; call 911 if the danger is immediate.

days.guide: The child writes a safety plan for a scenario.

questions.q: What goes into a dating violence safety plan?
questions.a: Trusted people to tell, safe places, code words, how to get help (911, loveisrespect: text LOVEIS to 22522 or call 1-866-331-9474), digital safety steps, documenting incidents.

weeks.assessment_key: Safety plan rubric: 4 = recognizes warning signs in the scenario, lists trusted adults and hotlines (loveisrespect 1-866-331-9474), safe places, digital safety steps, documentation, and 911 for danger; 3 = mostly complete; 2 = vague; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Phone and computer; NCMEC Take It Down (takeitdown.ncmec.org) and CyberTipline info; a grooming case study. Prepare a 3-scenario quiz.
misconceptions: Thinking privacy settings make posts private forever. Correct: anything posted can be screenshotted and shared.
Believing sextortion victims should pay. Correct: don't pay; save evidence, stop contact, tell an adult and report.

days.guide: Search the child's name together; review and tighten privacy settings.

questions.q: What is a digital footprint?
questions.a: The trail of data you leave online — posts, photos, comments, searches — which can be permanent and public.

days.guide: Explain sextortion and steps: stop responding, don't pay, save evidence, block, tell an adult, report to CyberTipline, use Take It Down.

questions.q: What does Take It Down do?
questions.a: A free NCMEC service that helps remove or stop the online sharing of nude or explicit images taken of someone under 18.

days.guide: Analyze the case study stages (targeting, trust, filling a need, isolation, sexualization, control) and practice blocking/reporting.

questions.q: What are early signs of online grooming?
questions.a: Excessive flattery, gifts, asking for secrecy, moving to private apps, asking personal questions, then requesting photos.

days.guide: Create a tech-use plan.

questions.q: Name one notification setting that improves wellbeing.
questions.a: Turn off non-essential notifications or use Do Not Disturb/Focus at night.

days.guide: Give the scenario quiz.

questions.q: How can you spot a phishing message?
questions.a: Urgent threats, unfamiliar sender, misspellings, requests for passwords or money, suspicious links.

weeks.assessment_key: Scenario quiz key: phishing — don't click, verify sender, report/delete; sextortion — don't pay or respond, save evidence, block, tell adult, report to NCMEC/Take It Down; oversharing post — remove location/school info, adjust privacy. Proficient: safest response for all three with reasons.

weeks.prep: Household items for a go-bag (water, flashlight, batteries, N95s, first aid, medications, document copies). Ready.gov kit list; AirNow.gov; MyShake app (California earthquake alerts).
misconceptions: Running outside during an earthquake. Correct: Drop, Cover and Hold On where you are.
Thinking cloth masks protect from wildfire smoke. Correct: a well-fitted N95 filters fine particles; cloth masks don't.

days.guide: Practice Drop, Cover, Hold On; identify safe spots (under sturdy tables) and hazards (windows, tall furniture).

questions.q: What should you do if there's no table?
questions.a: Drop near an interior wall, cover head and neck with your arms, hold on; stay away from windows.

days.guide: Learn Ready-Set-Go evacuation and AQI categories.

questions.q: What AQI level is unhealthy for everyone?
questions.a: 151–200 (red, Unhealthy); 101–150 is unhealthy for sensitive groups.

days.guide: Write the go-bag checklist and gather items.

questions.q: How much water per person?
questions.a: At least 1 gallon per person per day for several days (Ready.gov recommends a 3-day supply for evacuation, 2 weeks at home).

days.guide: Create the family plan with meeting points and contacts.

questions.q: Why have an out-of-area contact?
questions.a: Long-distance calls/texts often work when local lines are jammed.

days.guide: Present the plan; run a timed drill; note improvements.

questions.q: What should you do after shaking stops?
questions.a: Check for injuries, look for hazards (gas, fire), evacuate if unsafe, expect aftershocks and follow the family plan.

weeks.assessment_key: Family plan rubric: 4 = contacts incl. out-of-area, two meeting places, evacuation routes, go-bag checklist complete, roles assigned, drill run with improvements recorded; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = partial; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: First aid kit, pillow or manikin, AED demo video, CPR checklist and the Unit 6 test.
misconceptions: Removing a cloth soaked with blood. Correct: add more layers on top and keep pressure.
Putting ice or butter on burns. Correct: cool with cool running water for 10–20 minutes; cover loosely.

days.guide: Teach Check–Call–Care; practice a 911 call.

questions.q: What should you give a dispatcher first?
questions.a: Your exact location, then what happened and the number of victims; stay on the line.

days.guide: Practice cuts (gloves, direct pressure, bandage) and burns (cool running water, cover, don't pop blisters).

questions.q: How do you stop severe bleeding?
questions.a: Gloves if possible, firm direct pressure with gauze, add more layers if soaked, call 911; a tourniquet for life-threatening limb bleeding.

days.guide: Practice Hands-Only CPR to 'Stayin' Alive' (100–120/min, at least 2 inches).

questions.q: Where do you place your hands?
questions.a: Heel of one hand on the center of the chest (lower half of the breastbone), other hand on top.

days.guide: Watch AED video; sequence cards; pad placement: upper right chest below collarbone, lower left side below armpit.

questions.q: What is the first AED step?
questions.a: Turn it on and follow the voice prompts.

days.guide: Give the Unit 6 test and 2-minute CPR check.

questions.q: When should you stop CPR?
questions.a: When EMS or an AED takes over, the person shows signs of life, the scene becomes unsafe, or you are too exhausted.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 6 test key: leading teen causes of death; firearm storage; drowning signs; concussion law AB 2127; cycle of abuse; de-escalation; digital footprint; sextortion steps; Drop-Cover-Hold On; AQI levels; go-bag; Check-Call-Care; bleeding control; burn care (cool water 10–20 min); CPR rate/depth; AED pad placement. CPR checklist: scene safety, responsiveness, 911/AED, hand placement, 100–120/min, 2 inches, full recoil, minimal pauses (7–8 of 8 proficient).

weeks.prep: Glitter or lotion with glitter for handwashing demo; immune system diagram; California school immunization requirements (shotsforschool.org). Write quiz.
misconceptions: Thinking antibiotics cure viral infections like colds or flu. Correct: antibiotics only work on bacteria.
Believing vaccines cause the disease they prevent. Correct: vaccines contain weakened, inactivated or partial pathogens or instructions (mRNA) that train immunity without causing disease.

days.guide: Compare pathogens: bacteria (strep throat, TB), viruses (flu, COVID-19, measles), fungi (athlete's foot, ringworm), parasites (malaria, giardia).

questions.q: Give one disease for each pathogen type.
questions.a: Bacteria – strep throat; virus – influenza; fungus – athlete's foot; parasite – malaria (protozoan) or lice/tapeworms.

days.guide: Put glitter on hands, shake hands/touch objects, then compare washing methods (20 seconds with soap).

questions.q: How long should you wash hands?
questions.a: At least 20 seconds with soap and water.

days.guide: Diagram: first line (skin, mucus), innate (inflammation, white blood cells), adaptive (B cells → antibodies; T cells; memory cells).

questions.q: How do vaccines work?
questions.a: They expose the immune system to a harmless form or piece of a pathogen so it makes antibodies and memory cells, ready to respond fast to the real pathogen.

days.guide: Review CA requirements (Tdap booster for 7th grade) and recommended teen vaccines (HPV, meningococcal, flu, COVID-19).

questions.q: Which vaccine is required for California 7th-grade entry?
questions.a: Tdap booster (and varicella if not already immune).

days.guide: Give the quiz; child writes herd immunity paragraph.

questions.q: Explain herd immunity with a class of 30.
questions.a: If 27 of 30 students are immune, an infected student has few people to spread to, so the disease can't spread widely, protecting the 3 who can't be vaccinated.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: four pathogen types with examples; transmission routes (direct contact, droplets/airborne, contaminated food/water, vectors); handwashing 20 s; immune defenses; antibodies and memory cells; vaccines train immunity; antibiotics don't kill viruses; Tdap required for 7th grade. Herd immunity paragraph: 4 = explains immune majority blocks chains of transmission and protects vulnerable people with a numeric example.

weeks.prep: CDC fact sheets on heart disease, type 2 diabetes and cancer; family health history form; screening chart template (USPSTF/ACS guidance).
misconceptions: Thinking screenings are only for when you feel sick. Correct: screenings find problems early before symptoms.
Believing sunscreen is only needed on sunny days. Correct: UV passes through clouds; use SPF 30+ daily outdoors.

days.guide: Research risk factors: heart disease (smoking, high BP, high cholesterol, inactivity), diabetes (excess weight, inactivity, family history), cancer (tobacco, UV, alcohol, HPV).

questions.q: Name two controllable risk factors for heart disease.
questions.a: Smoking, inactivity, unhealthy diet high in saturated fat and sodium, excess weight, uncontrolled blood pressure.

days.guide: Interview a family member and record the history.

questions.q: Why does family history matter?
questions.a: Some conditions have genetic risk; knowing it guides earlier screening and prevention.

days.guide: Chart screenings and habits: blood pressure (yearly checkups), cholesterol (once between ages 9–11 and again 17–21 per AAP), skin checks, cervical screening starting at 21, testicular self-awareness.

questions.q: At what age does routine cervical cancer screening begin?
questions.a: Age 21 (Pap test every 3 years for ages 21–29).

days.guide: Learn dental care (brush twice, floss daily, checkups), vision checks, hearing protection (sounds above 85 dB), sun safety.

questions.q: What volume can damage hearing over time?
questions.a: Sounds at or above about 85 decibels with long exposure; keep earbuds below 60% volume.

days.guide: Child writes the prevention plan.

questions.q: What three habits lower chronic disease risk?
questions.a: Regular activity, a balanced diet, no tobacco (also sleep, limiting alcohol, sun protection).

weeks.assessment_key: Prevention plan: 4 = uses family history, names specific risks, three habits to start now with how to track, and age-appropriate future screenings; 3 = mostly complete; 2 = generic; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Three health product ads; glossary of insurance terms (premium, deductible, copay, coinsurance, out-of-pocket max, network); an OTC label (e.g., acetaminophen); medication/allergy list template.
misconceptions: Thinking a deductible is a monthly fee. Correct: the premium is the monthly fee; the deductible is what you pay for care before insurance starts paying.
Taking two products with the same active ingredient. Correct: check active ingredients to avoid overdose (e.g., acetaminophen in cold medicines and pain relievers).

days.guide: Evaluate claims and quackery red flags.

questions.q: Name two quackery red flags.
questions.a: Miracle cure, 'secret formula,' cures many unrelated conditions, only testimonials, pressure to buy now.

days.guide: Teach insurance terms; Medi-Cal (CA Medicaid, low/no cost) and Covered California (marketplace with subsidies).

questions.q: Define premium, deductible and copay.
questions.a: Premium: regular payment to have insurance. Deductible: amount you pay for covered care before insurance pays. Copay: fixed amount you pay for a visit or prescription.

days.guide: Compare brand vs. generic; read the OTC Drug Facts label (active ingredient, uses, warnings, directions).

questions.q: Where on an OTC label do you find the maximum dose?
questions.a: In the Directions section (and Warnings for overdose cautions).

days.guide: Prepare questions and a med/allergy list; role-play a visit.

questions.q: Give a good question for a doctor.
questions.a: 'What are the side effects of this medicine?' or 'When should I follow up?'

days.guide: Give the quiz with a deductible problem.

questions.q: Your deductible is $500 and you've paid $0 so far. A $1,200 bill comes; after the deductible you pay 20% coinsurance. What do you owe?

weeks.assessment_key: Consumer health quiz key: premium/deductible/copay/coinsurance/out-of-pocket max definitions; Medi-Cal vs Covered California; generics same active ingredient; OTC label sections; avoid doubling active ingredients; quackery red flags; sample: $500 deductible, 20% coinsurance on $1,200 → $640; $30 copay visit → pay $30.

weeks.prep: AirNow; your water supplier's Consumer Confidence Report (search supplier name + 'CCR'); CalEnviroScreen (oehha.ca.gov/calenviroscreen); county public health website. Write Unit 7 test.
misconceptions: Thinking pollution affects everyone equally. Correct: communities near freeways, ports and industry (often low-income and communities of color) bear more exposure.
Believing bottled water is always safer than tap. Correct: public tap water is regulated and tested; check the CCR.

days.guide: Check AQI; research effects of PM2.5 and ozone (asthma, heart and lung disease).

questions.q: What is PM2.5?
questions.a: Fine particles 2.5 micrometers or smaller that can enter deep into lungs and the bloodstream.

days.guide: Find the CCR; identify source and two contaminants vs. legal limits (MCLs).

questions.q: What is an MCL?
questions.a: Maximum Contaminant Level — the legal limit for a contaminant in drinking water.

days.guide: Explore CalEnviroScreen for your area and another.

questions.q: What does CalEnviroScreen show?
questions.a: Which California communities face the most pollution burden and population vulnerability, by census tract.

days.guide: Research county public health roles (disease surveillance, inspections, vaccines, emergency response).

questions.q: Give two jobs of a county public health department.
questions.a: Track and control disease outbreaks, inspect restaurants, run immunization clinics, issue health advisories, emergency preparedness.

days.guide: Give the Unit 7 test.

questions.q: Why can't antibiotics treat the flu?
questions.a: Influenza is a virus; antibiotics only kill bacteria (antivirals may help).

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 7 test key: pathogens; transmission; immunity and vaccines; herd immunity; chronic disease risk factors; screenings (cervical at 21); dental/hearing/sun safety; quackery; insurance terms and cost calculation; generics; OTC labels; PM2.5/AQI; CCR/MCL; CalEnviroScreen/environmental justice; county public health roles.

weeks.prep: Computer, poster board; advocacy rubric (accuracy, audience, persuasive appeal, call to action); citation help.
misconceptions: Picking a topic too broad. Correct: narrow to a specific problem and audience.
Forgetting the call to action. Correct: tell the audience exactly what to do.

days.guide: Child chooses a topic and writes a problem statement with audience.

questions.q: What makes a strong problem statement?
questions.a: It names a specific issue, who it affects, evidence of the problem and why it matters.

days.guide: Gather three credible sources, two stats and one expert recommendation with citations.

questions.q: Is a TikTok video a credible source?
questions.a: Not by itself; trace claims to .gov, .edu or peer-reviewed sources.

days.guide: Build the product.

questions.q: What is a call to action?
questions.a: A specific request telling the audience what to do (e.g., 'Ask the school board to start school after 8:30').

days.guide: Parent scores with rubric; child revises.

questions.q: Which rubric category was weakest and how did you fix it?
questions.a: Answers vary; look for a specific revision.

days.guide: Child presents and submits with works cited.

questions.q: How do you answer a question you don't know?
questions.a: Say you'll look it up and cite a credible source later.

weeks.assessment_key: Advocacy rubric (4 levels each): Accuracy — 3+ credible cited sources, correct statistics; Audience — message and format fit the audience; Persuasive appeal — uses evidence and emotion effectively; Call to action — specific, doable. Proficient = 3s across.

weeks.prep: Review packet; 30 unit flashcards; 25 practice questions; final exam; week-1 wellness inventory for retake; wellness plan template.
misconceptions: Cramming instead of retrieval practice. Correct: quiz yourself and fix errors.
Vague wellness goals. Correct: write SMART goals with tracking.

days.guide: Complete the units 1–4 review grid and flashcards.

questions.q: What's the difference between tolerance and dependence?
questions.a: Tolerance: need more for the same effect. Dependence: body relies on the drug and withdrawal occurs without it.

days.guide: Answer 25 practice questions on units 5–7; correct misses.

questions.q: What does AB 2127 require?
questions.a: Removal for the day after a suspected concussion, written clearance and at least a 7-day graduated return-to-play protocol.

days.guide: Write a wellness plan with SMART goals for physical, mental/emotional and social health.

questions.q: Give a SMART social goal.
questions.a: 'I'll join one club this semester and attend at least 3 meetings a month, tracked on my calendar.'

days.guide: Give the final exam.

questions.q: Name the steps of DECIDE.
questions.a: Define, Explore, Consider, Identify values, Decide, Evaluate.

days.guide: Retake the inventory; child writes a reflection comparing results.

questions.q: What changed most since week 1?
questions.a: Answers vary; should cite score changes and specific habits.

weeks.assessment_key: Final exam key draws on all unit keys: WHO health definition; DECIDE; SMART; CRAAP; six nutrients; 5/20 rule; stress hormones; ACT and 988; dopamine and addiction; Tobacco 21; BAC laws; fentanyl/naloxone; affirmative consent; contraception effectiveness; STI curable vs treatable; Title IX; drowning signs; concussion law; Drop-Cover-Hold On; CPR 100–120/min; vaccines; insurance terms. Essay: 4 = applies all DECIDE steps with realistic consequences and values. Wellness plan: 4 = three SMART goals with supports, obstacles and tracking.
